reference.source: Standard breast surgery textbook and benign breast disease guidance
clinicalPearls: Idiopathic granulomatous mastitis is a benign chronic inflammatory breast condition that characteristically mimics carcinoma both clinically and on imaging
It typically affects women of reproductive age, often within a few years of pregnancy or lactation, presenting with a firm, sometimes tender breast mass
Associated features can include skin inflammation, abscess formation, sinuses, fistulae, and nipple retraction, reinforcing the resemblance to inflammatory or locally advanced cancer
The diagnosis is one of exclusion, requiring core biopsy showing non-caseating granulomatous lobulitis and active exclusion of tuberculosis and other specific infections
Microbiological work-up, including tests for mycobacteria and, in some series, Corynebacterium species, is important before attributing the disease to an idiopathic cause
Because it can look identical to malignancy, triple assessment with core biopsy rather than fine-needle aspiration alone is essential to obtain architecture and exclude cancer

Management is generic and may include observation, anti-inflammatory or immunosuppressive treatment, and conservative handling of abscesses, with wide surgery avoided where possible because of poor wound healing and recurrence
The condition often follows a prolonged, relapsing course but is ultimately self-limiting in many women
reference.pathophysiology: Idiopathic granulomatous mastitis is characterised histologically by non-caseating granulomas centred on the breast lobules, formed by epithelioid histiocytes, multinucleate giant cells, and surrounding chronic inflammatory cells. The precise trigger is unknown, but it is thought to represent a localised immune-mediated reaction to extravasated luminal secretions or lobular antigens, sometimes with a contribution from Corynebacterium infection, and it is associated with recent pregnancy, lactation, and hyperprolactinaemic states. The inflammatory process can progress to microabscesses, sinuses, and fistulae. Crucially, the granulomatous appearance is shared with tuberculosis and other infections, so those must be excluded before the label of idiopathic disease is applied.
additionalDifferentials: Breast carcinoma, including inflammatory breast cancer
Bacterial breast abscess and periductal mastitis
additionalInvestigations: Core needle biopsy for histology showing non-caseating granulomatous lobulitis
Ultrasound and mammography as part of triple assessment
Microbiological testing including stains and culture for mycobacteria and bacteria
Screening for tuberculosis where clinically or epidemiologically relevant
Serum prolactin and assessment for causes of hyperprolactinaemia
Tests to exclude sarcoidosis or other systemic granulomatous disease when indicated
redFlags: Imaging or clinical features indistinguishable from malignancy pending biopsy
Caseating granulomas or other findings suggesting tuberculosis
Rapidly progressive skin involvement raising concern for inflammatory carcinoma
Systemic symptoms suggesting disseminated infection or sarcoidosis
Non-resolving disease despite treatment, warranting repeat biopsy
reference.prognosis: The condition is benign and often eventually self-limiting, but it is notorious for a protracted, relapsing course with recurrent inflammation and sinus formation; most women recover with conservative or medical management, though scarring can result.
pitfalls: Labelling the disease idiopathic without excluding tuberculosis and other infections
Relying on fine-needle aspiration and missing the granulomatous architecture or an underlying cancer
Undertaking wide surgical excision that heals poorly and tends to recur
Overlooking hyperprolactinaemia as a contributing factor
Mistaking the presentation for inflammatory breast carcinoma or vice versa
references: Standard breast surgery reference text on inflammatory breast conditions
management: Exclude carcinoma and specific infection first through triple assessment with core biopsy showing non-caseating granulomatous lobulitis, plus microbiological testing for mycobacteria before labelling disease idiopathic
Manage mild disease expectantly with simple analgesia and observation, as it is often eventually self-limiting
Use systemic or topical corticosteroids for symptomatic, extensive or rapidly progressive disease
Add a steroid-sparing immunosuppressant such as methotrexate for refractory or relapsing disease
Give targeted antibiotics where Corynebacterium species or another organism is identified on culture
Reserve surgery for abscess drainage or genuinely refractory localised disease, avoiding wide excision that can worsen scarring and sinus formation
Measure serum prolactin and address any cause of hyperprolactinaemia contributing to the condition
Refer to a breast multidisciplinary team and counsel on the protracted, relapsing course
